electrician.intro: Learn electrical work from first principles. Wire buildings safely, diagnose faults, and follow code. This is a trade that pays well, travels across borders, and never stops being in demand.

skillDomains.name: Electrical Theory
skillDomains.description: The foundation. Without this, every wire you pull is a guess.

skills.name: Basic Electricity
skills.description: Voltage, current, resistance, power — the four quantities behind every circuit.

modules.title: What is electricity?
modules.content:
Electricity is the flow of electrons through a conductor. Three quantities describe it:

  • Voltage (V) — the pressure pushing electrons
  • Current (A) — the rate of electron flow
  • Resistance (Ω) — what opposes the flow

They are linked by Ohm's Law: V = I × R.

Power (watts) is the rate of energy use: P = V × I.

Every calculation in electrical work comes from these two formulas.

modules.title: Ohm's Law in practice
modules.content:
Finding current

240V circuit with 60Ω resistance. I = 240 ÷ 60 = 4A.

Finding voltage drop

A 5A current through 2Ω of cable resistance causes V = 5 × 2 = 10V drop. On a 240V circuit, that's 4% loss — unacceptable for most circuits.

Finding power

240V × 10A = 2400W. That's why a 13A socket tops out at roughly 3000W.

Every size decision — cable, breaker, fuse — starts with one of these calculations.

steps.q: A 240V circuit draws 5A. What is the resistance?
A device draws 8A at 240V. What power does it use?
A 12V battery runs a 6W lamp. How much current?

modules.title: AC vs DC
modules.content:
Direct current (DC)

Flows one direction. Used by batteries, solar panels, electronics.

Alternating current (AC)

Reverses direction 50 times per second (50 Hz in most of West Africa). This is what the grid delivers and what most appliances use.

Why AC won

AC can be transformed to high voltage for transmission (low loss over distance), then stepped down for use. DC cannot be transformed as easily.

What this means for you

You'll work primarily with AC. But you'll encounter DC in battery backup, solar, and electronics. Know both.

skills.name: Circuit Types
skills.description: Series, parallel, and the two wiring systems used in homes.

modules.title: Series vs parallel
modules.content:
Series

Current flows through every component in turn. One break = whole circuit dead. Voltage divides between components. Used for switches, not for power circuits.

Parallel

Every component connects across the same supply. One break doesn't kill the others. Voltage is the same across all. Used for all power circuits in homes.

Rule

Every socket, light, and appliance in a house is wired in parallel. The series is only used for control circuits.

modules.title: Ring vs radial circuits
modules.content:
Radial circuit

Cable runs from the consumer unit to each socket in turn, ending at the last socket. Simple. Common in West Africa and most of the world.

Ring circuit

Cable runs from the consumer unit through all sockets and back to the consumer unit. Common in the UK and its former colonies (including Ghana). Carries more load on thinner cable because current can flow two ways.

You must know which system a property uses. Adding a socket the wrong way creates a fire risk.

steps.q: You find a cable running from the consumer unit through 6 sockets and back to the consumer unit. What system?
steps.f: A cable returning to the consumer unit is a ring circuit.

steps.q: A radial circuit uses 2.5mm² cable on a 20A breaker. How many sockets can it serve?
o: It depends on total load, not socket count
steps.f: Radial circuits are limited by total load, not socket count. Assess the actual current draw.

steps.q: A single light circuit runs from the switch through 5 lights in series. What happens when one bulb fails?
steps.f: Series circuits break entirely when one component fails. This is why lights are always wired in parallel.

skillDomains.name: Wiring
skillDomains.description: Cables, sizing, and the physical work of running circuits.

skills.name: Cable Selection
skills.description: Choose the right cable for the load, the environment, and the code.

modules.title: Common cable types
modules.content:
Twin and earth (T&E)

The standard for fixed wiring in dry locations. Two insulated conductors (live and neutral) plus bare earth.

Flexible cable

Stranded copper, used for appliances and pendants. Not for fixed wiring.

Armoured cable (SWA)

Steel wire armour for outdoor or underground runs. Protects from damage and moisture.

Single core

Used inside conduit. Common in industrial and some West African domestic installations.

Sizing

Cable size is measured in mm² of copper cross-section. Bigger cable = more current capacity and less voltage drop.

steps.q: A 13A socket circuit (typical domestic socket) needs what cable size?
steps.f: 2.5mm² is the standard for domestic socket circuits.

steps.q: A 6kW electric shower needs what cable size?
steps.f: 6kW at 240V = 25A. Requires 10mm² cable for the current and distance.

steps.q: You need to run cable 30m to a garden socket. Special consideration?
o: Use armoured cable and allow for voltage drop
steps.f: Long runs need armoured cable for physical protection and larger cable to overcome voltage drop.

skills.name: Installation
skills.description: The physical skill — routing, terminating, and mounting.

modules.title: Cable routing rules
modules.content:
Safe zones

Cables must run in defined safe zones so future drilling doesn't hit them:

  • Within 150mm of ceiling or floor
  • Within 150mm of a corner or wall
  • Vertically or horizontally from any accessory (socket, switch)

Never

  • Run diagonally across a wall
  • Bury in plaster without a capping
  • Run behind skirting without protection
  • Joint cables inside a wall

Every cable must be traceable and protected.

modules.title: Terminating cables
modules.content:
Stripping

Strip only what you need — usually 10-15mm of insulation. Too little = poor contact. Too much = exposed copper that can short.

Tightening

Terminals must be tight — loose terminals overheat and cause fires. But over-tightening damages the conductor. Use the correct screwdriver and firm, not excessive, force.

Colour codes (IEC)

  • Live — brown
  • Neutral — blue
  • Earth — green/yellow

Older installations may use different colours. Always verify with a tester.

steps.q: You see bare copper sticking out beyond the terminal screw. What's wrong?
o: Risk of short — strip should be precise
steps.f: Bare copper beyond the terminal can contact other conductors or the enclosure.

steps.q: A terminal screw feels loose after tightening. What do you do?
o: Replace the accessory — stripped threads mean it will never be safe
steps.f: A stripped terminal will overheat. Replace the whole accessory.

steps.q: IEC colour codes: which conductor is earth?
steps.f: Green/yellow is earth. Always.

modules.title: Document an installation
modules.prompt: Document a practice installation (real or simulated) with photos at each stage: cable routing, terminations, and final connection. Label each photo with what it demonstrates.

Photograph terminations showing correct strip length
Photograph the final connection at the consumer unit
Write a note on what you'd do differently next time

skillDomains.name: Testing & Safety
skillDomains.description: Prove it's safe before you leave. This is not optional.

skills.name: Isolation
skills.description: Make a circuit safe to work on.

modules.title: Lock off, prove dead
modules.content:
Before touching any conductor, you must:

  1. Identify the correct circuit
  2. Isolate at the consumer unit
  3. Lock off so nobody can restore power
  4. Post a warning at the isolation point
  5. Prove dead at the point of work with a tester

Never trust a switch. Never trust a label. Never trust the last person's word. Prove it yourself, every time.

steps.q: You've turned off a breaker. Can you start work?
o: No — prove dead at the point of work first
steps.f: Never trust the breaker. Prove dead.

steps.q: Your voltage tester shows no voltage but you're not sure it's working. What do you do?
o: Test the tester on a known live source first
steps.f: Prove the tester works, then prove the circuit is dead, then prove the tester again. This is the golden rule.

steps.q: You're called away mid-job. What do you do before leaving?
o: Keep isolation in place and warn others
steps.f: Isolation stays in place. Warn anyone on site. Never leave a partially-done job energised.

skills.name: Testing
skills.description: Measure and verify. Every installation must be tested before handover.

modules.title: The three essential tests
modules.content:
1. Continuity

Verify conductors are continuous and correctly connected. Earth continuity is the most critical.

2. Insulation resistance

Verify no leakage between conductors. Test with a 500V insulation tester between live-earth, live-neutral, neutral-earth.

3. Polarity

Verify live is live, neutral is neutral, earth is earth. Reversed polarity kills.

In industrial work you'll add loop impedance, RCD trip times, and more. But these three are the minimum for every domestic job.

steps.q: Earth continuity reads 0.05Ω on a 20m circuit. Acceptable?
o: Only if resistance is under 1Ω, so yes
steps.f: Earth continuity must be under 1Ω per circuit. 0.05Ω is excellent.

steps.q: Insulation resistance reads 0.5MΩ. What does this mean?
steps.f: Most standards require at least 1MΩ insulation resistance. 0.5MΩ indicates leakage.

steps.q: You test a socket and find live and neutral reversed. What does this cause?
o: Deadly risk — appliances remain live when switched off
steps.f: Reversed polarity means the appliance chassis stays live even when the switch is off. This kills people.

skillDomains.name: Fault Finding
skillDomains.description: Diagnose what's wrong without pulling the whole house apart.

modules.title: The diagnostic process
modules.content:
1. Ask the client — when did it start? What were you doing? Has anything changed?
  2. Narrow the scope — is it one socket or the whole circuit? One room or the whole house?
  3. Test at boundaries — where does power stop? That's where the fault lives.
  4. Isolate the section — split the circuit and test each half.
  5. Confirm and repair — once found, repair, retest, and verify the whole circuit.

Bad electricians replace parts and hope. Good ones diagnose.

steps.q: One circuit trips the breaker every time it rains. Most likely cause?
o: Water ingress into an outdoor cable or fitting
steps.f: Weather-dependent tripping means water is getting in. Find and seal the leak.

steps.q: A single socket doesn't work but everything else on the circuit is fine. First thing to check?
steps.f: Isolated faults are usually at the accessory. Open the socket and check terminations.

steps.q: The whole house loses power. Neighbour's house is fine. What's first?
steps.f: Isolated outage starts at your own consumer unit. Check the main switch, breakers, and RCD.

modules.title: Trace an intermittent fault
modules.prompt: A client reports that a bedroom socket works sometimes and not other times. It's been happening for weeks. Describe your systematic approach to find the fault.
modules.context: Intermittent faults are the hardest to find. Method matters more than tools.
rubric: Asks the client for patterns (time of day, weather, appliance use)
Tests the socket at both working and non-working times if possible
Checks terminal tightness first (most common cause)
Inspects for heat damage or arcing marks
Tests continuity of the cable run
Repairs the fault (retermination, replacement, or rewire)

skillDomains.name: Customer Work
skillDomains.description: Turn skill into income. Quotes, service, and running a business.

modules.title: What goes into a quote
modules.content:
1. Materials — cable, accessories, consumer units, fixings
  2. Labour — hours × your rate (never guess)
  3. Overhead — transport, tools wear, insurance
  4. Contingency — 10-15% for surprises
  5. Margin — 20-40% profit for the business

Most electricians under-quote by forgetting one of these. Then they work for free — or lose money.

modules.title: Quote a small rewire
modules.prompt: A client wants their 3-bedroom house rewired: 12 sockets, 8 lights, 4 switches, new consumer unit, and cable. Materials: 1,200,000 Le. Labour estimate: 5 days at 30,000 Le/day. Overhead: 50,000 Le. Contingency: 15%. Margin: 25%. Calculate the quote.
modules.context: Rewires are the biggest jobs most electricians quote. Getting the maths right determines whether you can run a business.

skills.name: Customer Service
skills.description: How to build a reputation that brings repeat work.

modules.title: Reputation is everything
modules.content:
In West Africa, electricians get work through word of mouth. One bad job costs ten future jobs.

Rules

  • Arrive on time, or call ahead
  • Explain what you're doing in plain language
  • Clean up after yourself
  • Test everything in front of the client
  • Give a written invoice
  • Offer a warranty on your work

A client who trusts you calls you first next time and refers you to friends.

modules.title: Build a customer service pack
modules.prompt: Design the materials you'll hand to every client: a written quote template, a service checklist for jobs, and an invoice. Make them professional and clear.
steps: Design a quote template with clear line items
Design a service checklist (what you check before leaving)
Design an invoice with payment terms
Test the pack on a real or simulated client
